messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 72
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 57

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Suppress Anger: never allow myself to feel or express anger, Avoid Circumstances: Being in circumstances that remind me of the event (eg, being in the dark)., Avoid Stressors: avoid anything that could be stressful
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.

Vignette:
At seventy-two, Mr. Tranh had spent the last forty years of his life caring for other people’s children. He was a nanny, a job he had taken after leaving his first wife, and one he had come to believe suited him precisely because it required him to be calm, patient, and gentle—everything he had not been allowed to be in his marriage. His second wife, Mei-Lin, knew only that he had been married before and that he did not like to talk about it. She had learned, over the years, not to ask.

The marriage that had shaped him ended one night in 1983, in the darkened bedroom of a small apartment in San Francisco’s Tenderloin. His first wife had been drinking—she drank often—and an argument had escalated into something familiar. She struck him first with her open hand, then with the heel of a shoe. He had learned, over the previous three years, that fighting back made things worse, so he had curled onto his side on the bed, his hands over his head, as she hit him again and again. What he remembered most vividly, even now, was not the pain but the position of his body: his knees drawn up, his chin tucked, his arms pressed against his skull. He remembered the smell of her breath and the way the streetlight through the blinds cast stripes across the wall. He remembered thinking, *this is not happening to me*. He had stayed in that position until she stopped and left the room, and then he had stayed there for another hour, unable to move.

He left her the next morning and never spoke of it.

But the memory did not leave him. It sat inside him like a stone, and over the decades, it had taken on a strange quality. When he thought about that night—which he tried not to—it felt as though it had happened to someone else. A different man, in a different life. And yet, when the memory surfaced unbidden, the terror was as fresh as it had been forty years ago. He would be folding laundry, or stirring a pot of soup, and suddenly his body would lock into that same curled position. His arms would press against his ribs, his chin would drop, and he would feel, for a few horrifying seconds, that he was back on that bed, waiting for the next blow. The physical sensation was so precise that it seemed almost impossible that the memory belonged to a stranger.

The consequences of that night had spread slowly into the rest of his life, like water soaking into dry cloth. He had become, he knew, a man who never let himself get angry. Not at the children he cared for, not at Mei-Lin, not at the drivers who cut him off on the street. Anger, he had learned, was dangerous. Anger was what had started the fights. Anger was what she had used as an excuse. So he had built a life around never feeling it. When a child threw a tantrum, he breathed slowly until it passed. When Mei-Lin criticised him, he nodded and said nothing. The anger was there—he could feel it, sometimes, a tightness in his chest—but he pushed it down so quickly and so completely that it might as well have not existed.

He had also learned to avoid anything that could be stressful. He turned down social invitations that might involve loud voices or disagreements. He stopped watching the news. He left the room when a television show included a scene of conflict. His world had become small and quiet, and he had convinced himself that this was peace.

But the peace was fragile. He had become hypervigilant in ways that exhausted him. A sudden movement nearby—a child running toward him, a door swinging open—would make him flinch as though he were about to be struck. The sound of a dropped pan in the kitchen would send his heart racing. He could not relax, even at home, even with Mei-Lin. He would sit in his armchair, ostensibly reading, but his shoulders never dropped, his jaw never unclenched. He was always waiting. He did not know what he was waiting for, only that it felt necessary.

His job had become difficult in ways he had not anticipated. The children he cared for, twin four-year-olds, were energetic and loud. Their sudden movements, their unexpected hugs from behind, their shrieks of laughter—all of it triggered that same startle response. He had begun to keep a distance from them, to position himself so that no one could approach him from the side. The mother had noticed. She had asked, gently, if he was feeling unwell. He had said he was fine.

What had finally brought him to a clinic was a moment three weeks ago. He had been walking home from the bus stop in the evening, and a car had backfired behind him. He had dropped to the ground. He had curled onto his side, his hands over his head, right there on the sidewalk. A stranger had asked if he needed an ambulance. He had said no, stood up, and walked home. But that night, he had not slept. He had lain in bed, rigid, staring at the ceiling, and for the first time in decades, he had let himself wonder if he was still living inside that bedroom.

He came to therapy because he was afraid of what might happen the next time a car backfired. He was afraid of losing his job. He was afraid of Mei-Lin finding out what had happened to him. But underneath all of that, what he wanted most was to feel, just once, that he was safe.
